query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The retention or loss of toughness in high-entropy alloys is governed by the formation of nano-twins and the resulting deformation modes, which can be influenced by the alloy composition and processing conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy with a random solid solution structure
generation.intervention: Controlled change in alloy composition, such as the addition of a specific element or modification of the processing conditions
generation.mechanism: Deformation modes, such as nano-twinning and dislocation slip, that alleviate the deleterious effects of high strength on toughness
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced toughness and strength-ductility synergy in high-entropy alloys with optimized composition and processing conditions
generation.baseline: Conventional high-entropy alloys with random solid solution structure
generation.boundary: Alloy composition, processing conditions, and temperature range
generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between nano-twinning, dislocation behaviors, and toughness in high-entropy alloys is not fully understood and requires further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Systematic investigation of the effect of alloy composition and processing conditions on nano-twinning and toughness in high-entropy alloys
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the formation of nano-twins does not correlate with enhanced toughness in high-entropy alloys, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: From the images in Fig. 3, the nano-twins in the EBSD scans become very clear by overlaying the scan on an image quality, IQ, map of the same data set, which permits the measurement of the typical misorientation angle of 60° for twinning (Fig. 3e). We conclude from these results that between room and cryogenic temperatures where the strength, ductility and toughness of the medium-entropy CrCoNi are all simultaneously enhanced, nano-twinning contributes an important additional deformation mode that helps alleviate the deleterious effects of high strength that would normally be expected to result in lower toughness.

Our results reveal that the heterogeneous lattice strain causes unusual dislocation behaviors (i.e., multiple kinks/jogs and bidirectional cross slips), resulting in the strengthening mechanisms that underpin the strength-ductility synergy. The outcome of our research sheds important insights into the design of strong yet ductile distorted crystalline solids, such as high-entropy alloys and high-entropy ceramics.

The exceptional mechanical strength of medium/high-entropy alloys has been attributed to hardening in random solid solutions. Here, we evidence non-random chemical mixing in a CrCoNi alloy, resulting from short-range ordering. A data-mining approach of electron nanodiffraction enabled the study, which is assisted by neutron scattering, atom probe tomography, and diffraction simulation using first-principles theory models. Two samples, one homogenized and one heat-treated, are observed. In both samples, results reveal two types of short-range-order inside nanoclusters that minimize the Cr–Cr nearest neighbors (L12) or segregate Cr on alternating close-packed planes (L11). The L11 is predominant in the homogenized sample, while the L12 formation is promoted by heat-treatment, with the latter being accompanied by a dramatic change in dislocation-slip behavior. These findings uncover short-range order and the resulted chemical heterogeneities behind the mechanical strength in CrCoNi, providing general opportunities for atomistic-structure study in concentrated alloys for the design of strong and ductile materials.
